Memorandum of Decision

of the

Honourable
Mr. Justice

R.A. Neufeld

_______________________________________________________

I.

Introduction

[
1
]

In this proceeding, the Applicants seek summary dismissal
(or, in the alternative, security for costs) in respect of actions brought
against them by the Respondent, Rosalina Templanza [Ms. Templanza]. They also
applied to have Ms. Templanza declared a vexatious litigant, per
Judicature
Act
, RSA 2000, c J-2, ss 23-23.1

[
2
]

Ms. Templanza’s actions relate back to a failed
attempt by Ms. Templanza to acquire a condominium in Calgary in the late 1990s,
and a claim subsequently brought by Ms. Templanza against her then lawyer.

[
3
]

The facts surrounding both of these matters are
set out in detail in the Alberta Court of Appeal decision of
Templanza v
Wolfman
,
2016 ABCA 1
at paras
3-24
, 612 AR 67, leave to appeal to SCC
refused, 36892 (15 September 2016).

[
4
]

To summarize, in 1998 Ms. Templanza wanted to
purchase a condominium, but could not qualify for a mortgage. Two of her
friends, Richard and Cecil Shields, came to her aid. They agreed to purchase
the condominium, and to then transfer it to Ms. Templanza, who would assume a
high ratio Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation [CMHC] mortgage on title. After
the purchase the Shields had second thoughts, and refused to transfer the
condominium, despite Ms. Templanza having arranged (with assistance from her
lawyer, Edward Wolfman) for CMHC to waive their personal covenant.

[
5
]

The Shields were represented by Mitchell Ford,
one of the current Defendants. A settlement was reached whereby the Shields
would convey the condominium to Ms. Templanza’s son, Eduardo Gabriel, who had
agreed to then convey it to his mother. Mr. Wolfman acted for both Ms.
Templanza and Mr. Gabriel.

[
6
]

Mr. Gabriel refused to authorize registration of
a transfer of land by Mr. Wolfman. He contended that his mother had not lived
up to her end of their agreement.

[
7
]

Mr. Wolfman ceased to act for either party. Ms.
Templanza retained the Defendant David Salmon, and, at a later point, the
Defendant John Anderson to bring lawsuits against Mr. Gabriel and then Mr.
Wolfman.

[
8
]

The claim against Mr. Wolfman was summarily
dismissed by Master Laycock, as being barred by the
Limitations Act
, RSA
2000, c L-12. Subsequent appeals by Ms. Templanza were dismissed. The appeal to
the Alberta Court of Appeal was heard in December 2015, and decided in January 2016:

Templanza v Wolfman
,
2016 ABCA 1
, 612 AR 67. The Supreme Court of Canada
then refused leave:
Templanza v Wolfman
, 36892 (15 September 2016)
(SCC).

II.

Current Litigation

[
9
]

The Statements of Claim currently before the
Court were filed by Ms. Templanza on November 2, 2015, approximately one month
before her appeal of the summary dismissal of the Wolfman action was heard.
They were also filed notwithstanding an Order of this Court denying leave to
amend the Statement of Claim against Mr. Wolfman to add the eight Defendants, which
led to an Order declaring Ms. Templanza to be in contempt.

[
10
]

The Defendants are or were lawyers, or their
respective law firms. Two of the eight lawyers are now deceased. One is
retired.

[
11
]

The Defendants can be divided into two groups.
The first is comprised of lawyers who represented parties adverse in interest
to Ms. Templanza, either during her failed attempt to acquire the condominium,
or in her action against Mr. Wolfman. The second is comprised of lawyers who
acted for her after Mr. Wolfman ceased to act due to a conflict of interest.

[
12
]

Each of the Defendants (or their litigation
representatives) swore Affidavits in support of the Applications. Ms. Templanza
chose not to conduct questioning on those Affidavits, but swore Affidavits of
her own, and was questioned on them.

[
13
]

I was appointed case management Justice in 2017.
In that capacity, I ordered that the actions be consolidated for the purpose of
case management.

[
14
]

I have also directed that any application to
amend the Statements of Claim so as to add additional Defendants will not be
heard until the current applications have been decided. This was in response to
Ms. Templanza sending correspondence to the Court to seek leave to add a number
of new Defendants to the actions, including:

1.         a lending institution that she
approached in the early 2000s in her effort to secure financing to purchase the
condominium;

2.          two of the lending
institution’s then employees, and

3.         Mr. Wolfman (once again).

Also in
abeyance is an unfiled application by Ms. Templanza requesting that she be
granted “Summary Trial with Juries” to be presided over by the Associate Chief
Justice.

III.

The Claims Against Counsel Acting for Parties
Adverse in Interest

i.

Mitchell Ford and Jason Ford

[
15
]

Action number 1501-13039 is brought by Ms.
Templanza against Mitchell Ford (and Mount Royal Law Office) and Jason Ford
(and Mount Royal Law Office). It was filed on November 2, 2015.

[
16
]

The Fords acted as legal counsel to Richard and
Cecil Shields during the April 2003 transfer of title to the condominium from
the Shields to Eduardo Gabriel, Ms. Templanza’s son, and in preceding
litigation by Ms. Templanza. They had no further involvement in the matter,
other than fielding requests from Ms. Templanza for production of their files
in 2014, and successfully opposing an application for production later that
year.

[
17
]

The Statement of Claim alleges that both Jason
and Mitchell Ford were engaged in a “scam” in 2001-2003 to steal the
condominium, together with Mr. Wolfman, the Defendant Mr. Salmon and the
Defendant Mr. Anderson. Ms. Templanza accuses them of theft, fraud and
conspiracy. She states that “Wolfman cannot do this crime alone without the
conspiracy of the Fords, et al” (para 17).

[
18
]

In an Affidavit dated March 21, 2017, Jason Ford
attests that Mitchell Ford acted for the Shields, including representing them during
the transfer of the condominium to Edurado Gabriel in 2003. He also states that
while he assumed conduct of the Shields matter after his brother’s death, he
has never represented Ms. Templanza, and has taken no action on the Shields
matter since 2003, “... save for defending myself in numerous applications made
against me by Templanza.”

[
19
]

He further attests that:

“I have no knowledge of, and did not
participate in, any scam, fraud, or conspiracy directed at the Plaintiff, or
which had the intended or actual effect of depriving the Plaintiff of any money
or property. I have no reason to believe that Mitchell had any involvement in
or participate in any scam, fraud or conspiracy directed at the Plaintiff, or which
had the intended or actual effect of depriving the Plaintiff of any money or
property.”

[
20
]

Ms. Templanza elected not to question Mr. Ford
on his Affidavit.

ii.

Alistair Taylor

[
21
]

Action Number 1501-13045 is brought against
Alistar (sic) Taylor and his former law firm Warren Tettensor Amantea.

[
22
]

The 1501-13045 Statement of Claim alleges that
at some time around the year 2000, Mitchell Ford “disappeared” and Mr. Taylor
took over the Shields matter. It alleges that “Alistar Taylore (sic) was ...
fully aware of the legal scam going on with Wolfman, Mitchell T. Ford, the
Shields and Templanza.”

[
23
]

The Statement of Claim also alleges that:

“Alistair Taylor sustained the fraud,
conspiracy, on going with the entire Templanza/Shield’s legal matter until such
time that Jason R. Ford is ready to take over of the Law Office of Mount Royal
Law Office. As it perfectly fit, in the way it is now.”

[
24
]

Mr. Taylor swore an Affidavit dated March 21,
2017 stating:

1.         that he has no recollection of
assisting in the transfer of files from Mitchell Ford to Jason Ford;

2.         that any such involvement would
have been of an administrative nature lasting less than one week;

3.         that he had never acted for Mr.
Templanza; and

4.         that:

“I have no
knowledge of, and did not participate in, and WBA did not participate in, any
scam, fraud, or conspiracy directed at the Plaintiff, or which had the intended
or actual effect of depriving the Plaintiff of any money or property.”

[
25
]

Ms. Templanza elected not to question Mr. Taylor
on his Affidavit.

iii.

Max Blitt

[
26
]

Action number 1501-13043 is brought against Max
Blitt and his law firm, Spier Harben Law Office. Mr. Blitt acts as counsel to
Eduardo Gabriel in defending an action brought by Ms. Templanza for recovery of
the condominium. The claim against Mr. Blitt is replete with anti-Semitic
comments, none of which will be repeated here.

[
27
]

The Statement of Claim alleges that Mr. Blitt
conspired with Mr. Wolfman, the Defendant Mr. Salmon and the Defendant Mr.
Anderson to cheat Ms. Templanza out of her condominium, and accuses him of
conspiracy, blackmail, fraud and criminal concealment of her rights towards
Eduardo Gabriel, Ms. Templanza’s son and current owner of the condominium.

[
28
]

By Affidavit sworn on March 29, 2017, Mr. Blitt
stated that the last step taken in the Gabriel action by the Defendants was
service of an Affidavit of Records on May 11, 2009. He says that a questioning
of Mr. Gabriel by Ms. Templanza was scheduled for March 19, 2012 but did not
proceed. Mr. Blitt swore that:

“Neither I nor Spier Harben have ever
represented or advised Templanza.

I have no knowledge of, and did not
participate in, and nor did Spier Harben participate in, any scam, fraud, or
conspiracy directed at the Plaintiff, or which had the intended or actual effect
of depriving the Plaintiff of any money or property.”

[
29
]

Ms. Templanza elected to not question Mr. Blitt
on his Affidavit. There was no further affidavit evidence before the Court as
to whether the action against Mr. Gabriel remains dormant. However, the Court
has recently set down for hearing an application by Ms. Templanza against Mr.
Gabriel for transfer of title of the condominium. That application will not be
affected by the applications at issue in this decision.

iv.

Douglas Stokes and Todd Lee (Miles Davison Law
Office)

[
30
]

Action number 1501-13040 was brought against
Douglas Stokes, Todd Lee and the Miles Davison law firm. The Miles Davison firm
was engaged by Mr. Wolfman to act in the defence of Ms. Templanza’s claim
against him. Mr. Stokes acted as counsel until his death in January 2012. Mr.
Lee took over the file at that time.

[
31
]

As previously indicated, the claim against Mr. Wolfman
was summarily dismissed in 2014, and Ms. Templanza’s various appeals were concluded
in September of 2016 when the Supreme Court of Canada refused leave to appeal.

[
32
]

The Statement of Claim against Mr. Stokes (and
Miles Davison) alleges that Mr. Stokes conspired with Mr. Wolfman, the
Defendant Mr. Salmon and the Defendant Mr. Anderson, as part of a scheme to have
Mr. Anderson intentionally miss the limitation period for bringing action
against Mr. Wolfman, and to “steal the condo as plotted”.

[
33
]

As part of the plot it is also alleged that the
Defendant Mr. Anderson conspired with Mr. Stokes and Mr. Lee by allowing time
to file a “bogus” Statement of Defence beyond the time set out in the
Alberta
Rules of Court
, Alta Reg 124/2010. Master Laycock of this court was also
allegedly involved in this conspiracy.

[
34
]

The Statement of Claim against Mr. Lee (and
Miles Davison in Action No. 1501-13040), filed on November 2, 2015 contains
similar allegations. For example, it states that:

“The skilled, systematic criminal and civil
offences of Todd Lee, and Miles Davison LLP and the entire Respondents are pre
meditated murder of the Plaintiff. By attacking and decapitating her mental
magnitude, and wallop her to physical destruction to her slow death in disguise
of agony for the entire legal matter in judicial sophistication of ceaseless
rigmarole ...

Todd Lee knew that Wolfman & Co., was
and is operating entirely in criminal capacity against an ignorant client of
his very own, while in the position of trust as a might shields. Todd Lee
should have meditated both since he took over from Doug Stokes, but he chose
not as per allocation of share as he knew that the Original Transfer of the
Condo is long well secured to the sharp and covetous claws of his client.
Therefore, Todd Lee is a willing participation of a role and conspiracy to
Wolfman, Salmon. Max Blitt, Anderson, Doug Stokes, Terrance Dawe, et al.”

[
35
]

Mr. Lee swore an Affidavit in support of these
applications on May 26, 2017. In it he attests that the last activity in the
Wolfman action which Ms. Templanza complains of was a cost award made in favor of
Wolfman on February 2013. He also states:

“I have no knowledge of, and did not
participate in, and Miles Davison LLP did not participate in, any scam, fraud,
or conspiracy directed at the Plaintiff, or which had the intended or actual
effect of depriving the Plaintiff of any money or property.”

[
36
]

Ms. Templanza elected not to question Mr. Lee on
this Affidavit, or on his more extensive Affidavit of March 20, 2017, sworn in
support of the application to have Ms. Templanza declared a vexatious litigant.

IV.

The Claims against Counsel Acting for Templanza

A.

David Salmon

[
37
]

Action No. 1501-13043 is brought against David
Salmon and his law firm, Salmon & Co. Mr. Wolfman received conflicting
instructions from Ms. Templanza and Mr. Gabriel regarding registration of a
Transfer of Land signed by Mr. Gabriel on June 7, 2005. Mr. Wolfman ceased to
act, and returned his file to Ms. Templanza in October 2006 (except for the
Original Transfer of Land).

[
38
]

Mr. Salmon was then retained by Ms. Templanza.
In May 2007, Mr. Salmon filed an originating application naming Mr. Gabriel as
a Respondent and seeking an Order transferring title to the condominium. In March
2008, Mr. Salmon withdrew as counsel. He recommended the Defendant Mr. John Anderson
to Ms. Templanza. She retained Mr. Anderson later that month.

[
39
]

The allegations contained in the Statement of
Claim included overbilling, conspiring with Mr. Wolfman, and at para 9:

“... to be blind and ignore with confidence
the bare fact of the executed consideration. This constitutes conspiracy, fraud,
and theft of legal fees.”

[
40
]

Mr. Salmon swore an Affidavit in support of the
Applications on March 23, 2017. In it he confirms having acted for Ms.
Templanza from May 1, 2007 to March 14, 2008. Ms. Templanza then moved her file
to Mr. John Anderson of the Dawe Law Office. Mr. Salmon states:

“I have no knowledge of, and did not
participate in, and Salmon & Company did not participate in, any scam,
fraud, or conspiracy directed at the Plaintiff, or which had the intended or
actual effect of depriving the Plaintiff of any money or property.”

[
41
]

Ms. Templanza elected not to question Mr. Salmon
on his Affidavit.

B.

John Anderson

[
42
]

Action No. 1501-13042 is brought against John
Anderson. Mr. Anderson practices as an associate in the Dawe Law Office. He was
engaged by Ms. Templanza in March 2008, and represented her until September 16,
2013 when he withdrew for non-payment of fees.

[
43
]

The Statement of Claim against Mr. Anderson
contains various allegations of fraud and conspiracy. He allegedly:

1.         intentionally failed to file a
Statement of Claim against Mr. Wolfman until it was too late;

2.         intentionally failed to sue Mr.
Salmon at all, and

3.         “... left behind Wolfman and
Salmon without a claim as a conspiracy for extortion and gobbling the condo and
the condo proceeds for every participant of a role per share.”

[
44
]

It is further alleged that Mr. Anderson told Ms.
Templanza that a Statement of Claim was filed against Wolfman and Salmon, but not
Gabriel. It is claimed that this was:

“... a blatant lie while in the position of
trust as documents at hand by the Plaintiff reveals their systematic fraud
conspiracy and all related criminal and civil offences.”

[
45
]

Mr. Anderson swore an Affidavit in support of
the Summary Dismissal application on March 24, 2017. He acknowledges acting for
Ms. Templanza in her action against Mr. Gabriel commencing in March 2008. He
states that he later received instructions to sue Mr. Wolfman, appending to his
Affidavit a handwritten note from Ms. Templanza dated April 28, 2009
instructing him to do so, and advising that “We are close to the 2 year
deadline to claim at Mr. Wolfman which is at the end of May”. He recalls
preparing the Statement of Claim and giving it to Ms. Templanza for filing, which
was done on May 22, 2009.

[
46
]

Regarding the alleged fraud, Mr. Anderson
attests:

“I have no knowledge of, and did not
participate in, and Dawe Law Office did not participate in, any scam, fraud, or
conspiracy directed at the Plaintiff, or which had the intended or actual
effect of depriving the Plaintiff of any money or property.”

[
47
]

Ms. Templanza elected not to question Mr.
Anderson on his Affidavit.

C.

Terrance Dawe (Dawe Law Office)

[
48
]

Action No. 1501-15265 is brought against
Terrance Dawe and his law firm, the Dawe Law Office.

[
49
]

The Statement of Claim against Mr. Dawe alleges
that as “senior legal entity” in this law office, Mr. Dawe had the capacity to
intervene with Mr. Anderson. It states at para 11 that:

“Terrance Dawe if never do so then he is a
willing participant of a role for Anderson’s criminal and civil offences from
March 4, 2008 until the final day of Anderson which officially ended on October
31, 2013.”

[
50
]

Mr. Dawe on March 17, 2017 swore an Affidavit in
support of his application for summary dismissal (and in the alternative
security for costs) and a vexatious litigant declaration.

[
51
]

In his Affidavit, he attests to having had no
personal involvement in the carriage of the actions against either Mr. Gabriel
or Mr. Wolfman. He states that:

“I have no knowledge of, and did not
participate in, and Dawe Law Office did not participate in, any scam, fraud, or
conspiracy directed at the Plaintiff, or which had the intended or actual
effect of depriving the Plaintiff of any money or property.”

[
52
]

Ms. Templanza elected not to question Mr. Dawe
on his Affidavit.

V.

Other Prospective Defendants

[
53
]

Since my appointment as Case Management Justice,
Ms. Templanza has attempted to file Amended Statements of Claim adding as Defendants
First Line Mortgage Inc., Helen Tymbos-Sanidas and Marilene Japa, Edward L.
Wolfman Professional Corporation, Edward L. Wolfman & Co., and Eduardo and
Shirley Gabriel.

[
54
]

As mentioned earlier, I directed that the
application to amend the various Statements of Claim will not be considered
until the current applications have been dealt with.

VI.

Materials Provided by Ms. Templanza

[
55
]

Ms. Templanza has sworn a number of Affidavits
in recent months:

1.         in response to the Applicants’
affidavits (whose styles of cause included the prospective new Defendants);

2.         in support of an application
for “Summary Trial with Juries”, to be presided over by the Associated Chief
Justice; and

3.         in support of an application
seeking my recusal.

The
recusal application has been already been considered and refused. The
Affidavits repeat the various allegations of criminal conspiracy and fraud
against the current Defendants and expand those allegations to include others
involved in Ms. Templanza’s failed attempt to purchase the disputed condominium
between 1999 and 2005.

[
56
]

Although the various affidavits were not
accepted for filing due to the inclusion of new Defendants in their style of
causes, questioning on Ms. Templanza’s unfiled affidavits in response to the
summary dismissal, security for costs, and vexatious litigant applications was
conducted, with permission of the Court. They were also provided to and
reviewed by me in advance of the hearing of these applications.

VII.

Summary Dismissal

A.

General Principles

[
57
]

The Defendants each apply for summary dismissal
of the Claims against them.

[
58
]

Summary judgment may be granted under
Rule

7.3(1) of the
Alberta Rules of Court
, which provides, in part:

7.3(1)   A party may apply to the Court for
summary judgment in respect of all or part of a claim on one or more of the
following grounds:

...

(b) there is no merit to a claim or part of
it; ...

[
59
]

In
Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd
,

2014 ABCA 108
, 371 DLR (4th) 339, the Alberta Court of Appeal noted that the
test for summary dismissal under
Rule
7.3 has been modified in light of
the “culture shift” mandated in the Supreme Court of Canada’s decision in
Hryniak
v Mauldin
,
2014 SCC 7
, [2014] 1 SCR 87:

... a fair and just adjudication, if it
provides a process that allows the judge to make the necessary findings of
fact, apply the law to those facts, and is a proportionate, more expeditious
and less expensive means to achieve a just result than going to trial.

...
summary judgment

rules must be interpreted broadly, favouring proportionality and fair access to
the affordable, timely and just adjudication of claims ...

(
Hryniak v Mauldin
, at paras
4-5
)

The modern test for summary judgment is ...
to examine the record to see if a disposition that is fair and just to both
parties can be made on the existing record.

New R. 7.3 calls for a more holistic
analysis of whether the claim has “merit”, and is not confined to the test of a
“genuine issue for trial” found in the previous rules.

(
Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway
,
at paras 13-14)

[
60
]

A trial is not required where a judge or master
is able to reach “a fair and just determination on the merits”, which is “... when
the process (1) allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact, (2)
allows the judge to apply the law to the facts, and (3) is a proportionate, more
expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result.”:
Hryniak v
Mauldin
, at para
49
. What is required is “confidence that she can find the necessary
facts” to reach the conclusion: para 50.

[
61
]

This animating principle of judicial economy can
also be found in foundational
Rule
1.2 of the
Rules of Court
. The
purpose of the rules is fair and just resolution of claims “... in a timely and
cost-effective way.” This is not just an objective, but an obligation on the
parties:
Rule
1.2(3).

[
62
]

The Court of Appeal has stated that “no merit” is
to be interpreted as follows:

From a substantive perspective, summary
judgment can be granted if, in light of what that fair and just process
reveals, there is no merit to the claim. No “merit” means that, even assuming
the accuracy of the position of the non-moving party as to any material and
potentially decisive matters- matters which would usually require ordinary forensic
testing through a trial procedure with viva voce evidence and which could not
be resolved through the fair and just alternative- the non-moving party’s
position viewed in the round has no merit in law or in fact.

Stated another way, in order for the
non-moving party’s case to have merit, there must be a genuine issue of a potentially
decisive material fact in the case which cannot be summarily found against the
non-moving party on the record revealed by the “fair and just process”. The
mere assertion of a position by the non-moving party in a pleading or
otherwise, the mere hope of the non-moving party that something will turn up at
a trial, does not suffice. The key is whether the circumstances require a viva
voce evidence in order to properly resolve the case. (
776826 Alberta Ltd
(cob Budweiser Motorsports Park) v Ostrowercha
,
2015 ABCA 49
at paras
10-11
,
593 AR 391).

[
63
]

In
Stoney Tribal Council v Canadian Pacific
Railway
,
2017 ABCA 432
at para
12
the majority decision stressed that the
threshold for summary judgment is a clear and easily applied standard, and that
a judge or master hearing a summary judgment application should not engage in
“... an assessment of the relative strength of the positions of the moving and
non-moving party. ...”.

[
64
]

A party who resists a summary judgment
application must “put its best foot forward” and  cannot rely on vague
assertions that more or better evidence might turn up if the matter was sent to
trial:
Canada (Attorney General) v Lameman
,
2008 SCC 14
at paras
11
, 19,
[2008] 1 SCR 372.

[
65
]

Certain factual disputes do not block a summary
judgment application, including:

•

a “bare denial” or “bald allegation” (
Canada
(Attorney General) v Lameman
, at para
11
;
Shefsky v California Gold
Mining Inc
,
2016 ABCA 103
at para
113
, 616 AR 290);

•

self-serving affidavit evidence unsupported by
other evidence (
Guarantee Co of North America v Gordon Capital Corp
,

1999 CanLII 664 (SCC)
, [1999] 3 SCR 423 at 436-37;
Shefsky v California Gold Mining Inc
, at
para
113
);

•

evidence that flies in the face of the record (
Dagher
v Glenn
,
2016 ABCA 38
at paras
30-32
;
Pioneer Exploration Inc (Trustee
of) v Euro-Am Pacific Enterprises Ltd
,
2003 ABCA 298
at para
25-26
, 27 Alta
LR (4th) 62); and

•

conflicting evidence which is not material to
the outcome of the summary judgment (
Lydian Properties Inc v Chambers
,

2009 ABCA 21
at paras
2
, 22-23, 457 AR 211;
Goodswimmer v Canada (Attorney
General)
,
2017 ABCA 365
at para
40
).

B.  Analysis and Conclusion

[
66
]

Although the legal and factual relationships
between the Defendants and the Plaintiff vary, the underlying fundamental claim
put forward is the same: the Defendants were part of a fraudulent conspiracy to
deprive Ms. Templanza of a condominium.

[
67
]

There is no need for
viva voce
evidence
to properly resolve these claims against the Defendants, as there is no genuine
issue of a potentially decisive material fact that cannot be summarily decided
on the documentary record before the Court. There are sufficient facts on the
record at this stage to determine whether the claims have any prospect for
success, including whether they are barred by the
Limitations Act
; and
it is unnecessary for the purpose of this application to go further than that.

1.         Defendants
Who Acted for Parties Adverse in Interest

[
68
]

As discussed earlier, this group of Defendants
is comprised of the Ford brothers and Messrs. Taylor, Blitt, Stokes, and Lee,
and their respective law firms.

[
69
]

At the outset it should be noted that the claims
against these Defendants appear to have no substance, in law or in fact.

[
70
]

There is, and was, no privity of contract
between these Defendants and the Plaintiff. As noted in
Lawerence v Sandilands
,

2003 BCSC 211
, a lawyer owes certain ethical duties to the Court, but the only
party to whom a solicitor owes an actionable duty is to her or his client. This
principle was endorsed by Manderscheid J in
Wong v Leung
,
2011 ABQB 688

at paras
23-24
, 530 AR 83, where he concluded:

“There can be
absolutely no legal duty of care owed by a Defendant's counsel to a Plaintiff.
If such duty were to exist, it would strike at the very heart of the
adversarial system, which forms the very foundation of litigation under the
common law. ...”

[
71
]

Moreover, to found a duty of care outside of the
solicitor/client relationship would require foreseeable harm arising from a
lawyer’s conduct, and sufficient proximity between the lawyer and the
non-client, third party to create a reasonable expectation that a lawyer would
be acting in a way to protect that person’s interest (
O’Connor Associates Environmental
Inc. v MEC OP LLC
,
2014 ABCA 140
at paras
19-20
, 572 AR 354).

[
72
]

In this case, there is no basis to argue that
any of the Defendants who have acted as counsel to parties who had been sued
(or threatened to be sued) by Ms. Templanza owed her a duty of care that might
give rise to liability in tort. None of them had a contractual relationship
with her, either.

[
73
]

The closest that the claims might come to
raising issues of actionable conduct is with respect to the allegations of
fraud. However, while each Statement of Claim is rife with allegations of
fraud, it is difficult, if not impossible, to discern what facts Ms. Templanza
relies upon to establish fraud.

[
74
]

For example, a common theme in the pleadings,
affidavits, and in oral submissions before the Court was that the Defendants
Stokes, Lee and Anderson must have been involved in a conspiracy for Mr.
Anderson to have (allegedly) missed the limitation period for commencing an
action against Mr. Wolfman. Ms. Templanza says that without a conspiracy
against her the limitation period would certainly have been met. This
illustrates how rather than pleading facts in support of the allegation, the
Statements of Claim offer circular reasoning.

[
75
]

For the Defendants Jason and Mitchell Ford the
alleged fraud is even more remote, dating back to their engagement on behalf of
Richard and Cecil Shields. Virtually no facts were pled to support the
allegations. Similarly, the claim against Mr. Blitt alleges without supporting
facts that Mr. Blitt conspired with Mr. Wolfman to “steal” the condominium in
2005, and arranged a fraudulent settlement meeting with Mr. Salmon in 2007 in
furtherance of the scheme. The fraud claim against Alistair Taylor, whose only
involvement was to assist in the transition of Mitchell Ford’s practice to Jason
Ford’s over a week or so following Mitchell Ford’s death, is also completely
unsupported by facts.

[
76
]

This offends two principles. First, a litigant
has no obligation to respond to and refute bald and unsubstantiated
allegations:
Canada (Attorney General) v Lameman
;
Shefsky v
California Gold Mining Inc
. Second, some of these pleadings offend the
Rule
in kisikawpimootewin
(
kisikawpimootewin v Canada
,
2004 FC 1426
at
paras
8-9
, 134 ACWS (3d) 396), that litigation is an abuse of court processes
when a “... defendant cannot know how to answer, and a court will be unable to
regulate the proceedings ...”, “bare assertions and bald statements” leave the
defendant “... both embarrassed and unable to defend itself ...”, and the court
is unable to identify the intended argument and/or specific material facts, see
also
R v Fearn
,
2014 ABQB 233
at para
23
, 586 AR 182;
Arabi v Alberta
,

2014 ABQB 295
at paras
85-86
, 589 AR 249;
Lee v Canada (Attorney General)
,

2018 ABQB 40
at paras
135
, 141. As Gill J observed in
Arabi v Alberta
,
there is no need for a court or responding litigant to answer to claims that
are “gibberish”, which “simply make no sense”, or which are “illogical,
impenetrable claims”.

[
77
]

Even if it is assumed, for the purpose of
argument, that the claims of fraud are triable as against this group of Defendants,
they are each barred by the
Limitations Act
.

[
78
]

The Defendant Mitchell Ford, who acted for the
Shields, attested to having had no contact with the matters in issue since
2003.

[
79
]

Mr. Stokes died in January 2012, when Mr. Lee
took over conduct of the defence of the claim against Mr. Wolfman. The injury
purportedly caused by the alleged conspiratorial conduct complained of by Ms.
Templanza, the allegedly intentional missing of the limitation period by Mr.
Anderson for suing Mr. Wolfman, took place at the latest in June 2011, when
counsel for Mr. Wolfman filed for summary dismissal. The conspiratorial conduct
alleged against Mr. Blitt centres on events that took place in 2005-2007,
although he continues to act for Mr. Gabriel to this day.

[
80
]

In response to the Defendants’ limitations
argument, Ms. Templanza argued that the fraud against her had been concealed. Her
pleadings sometimes refer to “fake limitations periods”. However, there is no
basis in fact disclosed in the pleadings to support a concealment argument. This
argument was rejected by the Court of Appeal in
Templanza v Wolfman
in
the course of upholding the summary dismissal of Ms. Templanza’s claim against
Mr. Wolfman. At para 23, the Court of Appeal concluded that May 9, 2007 marks
the point from which Ms. Templanza’s injury became known:

“... by May 9, 2007 at the latest, Templanza
had actual knowledge that she had suffered an injury as a result of Wolfman’s
alleged breaches of his duties as her lawyer. By this date, she knew that he
(1) had failed to protect her legal rights in respect of the condominium title;
(2) had failed to release the transfer of land to her or to her new lawyer for
registration; and (3) had failed to comply with her instructions to him that he
register the transfer of land. Further, Templanza knew that these alleged
breaches were attributable to the conduct of her former lawyer, Wolfman, and
that the alleged breaches of his duty to her warranted bringing a proceeding. ...
in order to meet the time limitations under the
Limitations Act
, Templanza
would have had to commence her action against the Wolfman defendants by no
later than May 9, 2009. But she failed to do so.”

[
81
]

Nor was this injury concealed: para 24.

[
82
]

The same reasoning
applies here. The claim against the Defendants Mitchell Ford, Jason Ford,
Alistair Taylor, Max Blitt, Doug Stokes, Todd Lee, and their respective law
firms are all therefore dismissed on this second, independent, basis.

2.         Defendants
Who Acted as Counsel to Ms. Templanza

[
83
]

The remaining group of Defendants are David
Salmon, Terrance Dawe, John Anderson and their respective law firms. Mr. Salmon
succeeded Mr. Wolfman as counsel to Ms. Templanza. Mr. Anderson succeeded Mr.
Salmon. Mr. Dawe is a partner in Mr. Anderson’s firm.

[
84
]

The legal relationship between the Plaintiff and
these Defendants was quite different. As counsel to Ms. Templanza, these Defendants
owed her both a contractual and professional duty of care, which they
acknowledge.

[
85
]

Mr. Salmon last acted for Ms. Templanza in March
2008. To that point, his chief involvement was he filed an originating
application for an Order transferring the condominium from Mr. Gabriel to Ms.
Templanza. Conduct of that matter was then transferred to Mr. Anderson.

[
86
]

The limitation period for bringing an action
against Mr. Salmon commenced to toll no later than March 14, 2008, and expired
no later than March 14, 2010.

[
87
]

There is no basis in fact or law to extend that
date due to fraudulent concealment. Ms. Templanza’s perceived injury - her
inability to secure title to the condominium - had been known since 2005, if
not earlier.

[
88
]

Mr. Anderson (and his law firm Dawe Law Office)
assumed conduct of the action against Mr. Gabriel, and later commenced an
action against Mr. Wolfman. The Wolfman action was dismissed as being barred by
the
Limitations Act
.

[
89
]

Initially Mr. Anderson acted as counsel and
represented Ms. Templanza during her opposition to the summary dismissal
application, but he ceased to act September 16, 2013 for non-payment of fees.
Ms. Templanza subsequently represented herself before Master Laycock and Justice
Poelman of this Court, before the Court of Appeal, and in a written application
for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.

[
90
]

While Mr. Anderson acted for Ms. Templanza until
September 16, 2013, the Statement of Claim against Mr. Anderson is centered on
the allegation that he fraudulently missed the limitation period for suing Mr.
Wolfman. Based on that claim, the remedies sought include:

1.         a declaration of ownership of the condominium,

2.         closure of the Dawe Law Office,

3.         disbarment of Mr. Anderson,

4.         general damages of $2,000,000,

5.         damages in lieu of specific performance of $4,000,000, and

6.         pre-judgment interest.

[
91
]

In the circumstances, I conclude that although
the solicitor/client relationship continued until September 16, 2013, the
injury complained of was known at the latest on July 12, 2011, when Ms.
Templanza swore an Affidavit responding to the Wolfman summary dismissal application.
In the ordinary course, the action against Mr. Anderson would need to have been
commenced at the latest by July 12, 2013; approximately 28 months prior to when
it was actually commenced (on November 2, 2015). The claim is therefore barred
by
section 3
of the
Limitations Act
.

[
92
]

The Defendant Terrance Dawe attested to having
had no personal involvement in the Templanza matter. The Statement of Claim
against him does not provide a factual basis for its assertion that Mr. Dawe
was involved in the conspiracy to fraudulently take her condominium or to
deliberately miss the limitation period for suing Mr. Wolfman. It is therefore
dismissible on that basis as based on bald allegations or per the
Rule in

kisikawpimootewin
.

[
93
]

The action against Mr. Dawe is, in any event,
also barred by
section 3
of the
Limitations Act
for the same reasons
that apply to the claim against Mr. Anderson.

VIII.

Vexatious Litigant Application

A.

Jurisdiction

[
94
]

The Applicants have applied to have the
Plaintiff declared a vexatious litigant, per
Judicature Act
, ss 23-23.1.
These provisions permit an application that:

23(1) ... the Court order that:

(a) the person
shall not institute a further proceeding or institute proceedings on behalf of
any other person, or

(b) a proceeding
instituted by the person may not be continued,

without the permission of the Court.

[
95
]

This step may occur where the “...
Court is satisfied that a person is instituting vexatious
proceedings in the Court or is conducting a proceeding in a vexatious manner
... “.

Judicature Act
, s 23(2) then identifies a non-exclusive
list of seven examples of “...
instituting vexatious
proceedings or conducting a proceeding in a vexatious manner ...”.

[
96
]

The
Judicature Act
procedure has in the
past been considered the only basis by which a person may apply to have an
individual made subject to court access restrictions as a so-called “vexatious
litigant”. However, since 2016, this Court has adopted a line of cases from the
UK Court of Appeal (
Ebert v Birch & Anor
, [1999] EWCA Civ 3043 (UK
CA) and
Bhamjee v Forsdick & Ors (No 2)
, [2003] EWCA Civ 1113 (UK
CA)) which conclude that this Court, as a superior court of inherent
jurisdiction, has as part of it inherent jurisdiction the authority to impose
court access restrictions on abusive litigants:
Hok v Alberta
,
2016 ABQB
651
at paras
14-25
, 273 ACWS (3d) 533, leave denied
2017 ABCA 63
, leave to
appeal to SCC refused, 37624 (2 November 2017);
1985 Sawridge Trust v
Alberta (Public Trustee)
,
2017 ABQB 548
at paras
42-53
.

[
97
]

The
Hok v Alberta
approach to court
access restrictions has subsequently been applied in:
Thompson v
International Union of Operating Engineers Local No. 955
,
2017 ABQB 210
at
para
56
, 278 ACWS (3d) 46, affirmed
2017 ABCA 193
;
Ewanchuk v Canada
(Attorney General)
,
2017 ABQB 237
at paras
92-96
, 54 Alta LR (6th) 135, appeal
abandoned Edmonton 1603-0287AC (Alta CA);
Ellis v Wernick
,
2017 ONSC
1461
at paras
6-12
;
McCargar v Canada
,
2017 ABQB 416
at para
110
;
1985
Sawridge Trust v Alberta (Public Trustee),

2017 ABQB 436
at para
58
;
1985
Sawridge Trust v Alberta (Public Trustee)
,
2017 ABQB 548
at paras
42-79
;
Re
Gauthier
,
2017 ABQB 555
at paras
69
, 84;
Onischuk v Edmonton (City)
,

2017 ABQB 647
at paras
34-35
;
MacKinnon v Bowden Institution
,
2017 ABQB
654
at para
70
;
Onischuk (Re)
,
2017 ABQB 659
at paras
62-66
;
McCargar
v Canada
,
2017 ABQB 729
at para
58
;
Lee v Canada (Attorney General)
,

2018 ABQB 40
at para
271
;
Loughlin v Her Majesty the Queen
,
2018 ABQB 45

at paras
40-41
;
Rothweiler v Payette
,
2018 ABQB 134
at para
36
;
MacKinnon
v Bowden Institution
,
2018 ABQB 144
at para
3
.

[
98
]

Ebert v Birch & Anor
concludes that legislation such as the
Judicature Act
, ss
23-23.1 was enacted based on a misconception that, historically, it was only
via legislation such as the
Judicature Act
and its antecedents that UK
tradition courts acquired the capacity to limit an abusive litigant’s court
filings intended to initiate a new proceeding or process, or which occurred in
a matter other than an action where litigation misconduct had occurred.

[
99
]

In many senses, this means the
Judicature Act
,
ss 23-23.1 procedure is, for this court, obsolete, or at best duplicative of
the authority vested in the Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench as a consequence of
its inherent jurisdiction to control its proceedings, and mitigate and minimize
abuse of its processes.
Ebert v Birch & Anor
concludes that
legislation which authorizes court access restrictions co-exists as an
alternative, parallel authority to the courts’ inherent jurisdiction. That
principle was also adopted in
Hok v Alberta
.

[
100
]

The modern
Hok v Alberta
approach to
control of abusive litigation is prospective, rather than punitive. A court
which evaluates whether court access limitations are appropriate asks what can
be anticipated from a litigant:

... when a court considers limits to future
court access by a person with a history of litigation misconduct the key
questions for a court are:

1.         Can
the court determine the identity or type of persons who are likely to be the
target of future abusive litigation?

2.         What
litigation subject or subjects are likely involved in that abuse of court
processes?

3.         In
what forums will that abuse occur?

(
Hok v Alberta
, at para 36)

[
101
]

As Thomas J observed in
1985 Sawridge Trust v
Alberta (Public Trustee)
, at paras 42-79, this prospective application of
the Court’s inherent jurisdiction is preferable to the
Judicature Act

procedure in many ways:

1.         the
Judicature Act

requirement for “persistent” misconduct means court actions “play ‘catch up’
with historic patterns of excuse”;

2.         the
Judicature Act

process fails to account for statements of intent and demeanor;

3.         intervention for worst-case
litigants occurs too late and only after widespread abusive of court processes,
other litigants, and self-injury to the abusive litigants themselves;

4.         certain abusive litigant’s
actions are the result of mental health issues which either distort the
litigant’s perceptions, or are examples of an identified psychiatric condition,
querulous paranoia; and

5.         some litigants, particularly
those who advance Organized Pseudolegal Commercial Arguments [“OPCA”] (
Meads
v Meads
,
2012 ABQB 571
, 543 AR 215), predictably engage in bad litigation
motivated by ideology and political belief.

[
102
]

Though the “vexatious litigant” application in
this action was initiated under the auspices of
Judicature Act
,
ss
23-23.1, I will now proceed to consider whether Ms. Templanza should be subject
to court access restrictions under this Court’s inherent jurisdiction. These
are parallel authorities that are equally available to this Court, see also
R
v Olumide
,
2017 ABCA 366
at para
3
;
Bourque v Tensfeldt
,
2017 ABCA
356
at para
6
;
Lofstrom v Radke
,
2017 ABCA 362
at para
8
.

[
103
]

In my view an inherent jurisdiction, prospective
litigation misconduct analysis provides a more robust, functional, and
efficient response to control of problematic litigants. Application of this
Court’s inherent jurisdiction is also consistent with
Hryniak v Mauldin

“culture shift” that courts should develop and employ methodologies which
achieve just, efficient, and proportionate responses, reaffirmed and reinforced
in
R v Jordan
,
2016 SCC 27
, [2016] 1 SCR 631;
R v Cody
,
2017 SCC
31
, 411 DLR (4th) 619.

[
104
]

The “culture shift” is especially relevant where
a self-represented litigant is involved (
Trial Lawyers Association of
British Columbia v British Columbia (Attorney General)
,
2014 SCC 59
at para

88
, [2014] 3 SCR 31), and where that self-represented litigant abuses the court
and its processes:
Ewanchuk v Canada (Attorney General)
, at para
88
.
Lawyers are expected to conduct themselves as officers of the Court, and are
answerable for misconduct to governing law societies. Self-represented litigants
do not carry such obligations and constraints and Courts need to be able to
undertake proactive measures to control and prevent abuse.

B.  Indicia of Litigation
Misconduct

[
105
]

Alberta and other Canadian courts have
identified characteristic features of abusive litigation which are a potential
basis for a Court to intervene and place court access restrictions on a
litigant. In Alberta
Chutskoff v Bonora
,
2014 ABQB 389
, 590 AR 288,
affirmed
2014 ABCA 444
is the leading case that identifies these “indicia” of litigation
misconduct. At para 92 Michalyshyn J identifies eleven categories.
Any

of these is a basis for a court to potentially intervene and order court access
restrictions.

[
106
]

Subsequent to
Chutskoff v Bonora
, a
number of other indicia categories have been identified in Canadian court
decisions:

1.         using court processes to
further illegal activities (
Re Boisjoli
,
2015 ABQB 629
at paras
98-103
,
29 Alta LR (6th) 334;
Rothweiler v Payette
,
2018 ABQB 134
at para
35
);

2.         “judge shopping” (
McCargar v
Canada
,
2017 ABQB 729
at para
9
;
Re
Onischuk
,
2017 ABQB 659
at para

18
);

3.         where a litigant indicates an
intention to engage in future abuse of court processes (
Lofstrom v Radke
,

2017 ABCA 362
at para
8
;
Van Sluytman v Muskoka (District Municipality)
,

2018 ONCA 32
at paras
23-24
);

4.         where litigation has a
political focus and is directed to acknowledgement and correction of perceived
government shortcomings, rather than asserting a right recognized in law (
Van
Sluytman v Muskoka (District Municipality)
, at paras
23-24
); and

5.         where the litigant minimizes or
dismisses litigation defects and abuse on the basis the person is a
self-represented litigant (
Van Sluytman v Muskoka (District Municipality)
,
at paras
23-24
).

[
107
]

When considering court access restrictions a
judge may refer to other external evidence, including:

1.         activities both inside and
outside of the courtroom (
Bishop v Bishop
,
2011 ONCA 211
at para
9
, 200
ACWS (3d) 1021, leave to appeal to SCC refused, 34271 (20 November 2011);
Henry
v El
,
2010 ABCA 312
at paras
2-3
, 5, 193 ACWS (3d) 1099, leave to appeal to
SCC refused, 34172 (14 July 2011));

2.         the litigant’s entire public
dispute history (
Thompson v International Union of Operating Engineers Local
No 995
,
2017 ABCA 193
at para
25
), including:

a) litigation in other jurisdictions (
McMeekin v Alberta
(Attorney General)
,
2012 ABQB 456
at paras
83-127
, 543 AR 132;
Curle v
Curle
,
2014 ONSC 1077
at para
24
;
Fearn v Canada Customs
,
2014 ABQB
114
at paras
102-105
, 586 AR 23);

b) non-judicial proceedings (
Bishop v Bishop
, at para
9
;
Thompson
v International Union of Operating Engineers Local No 995
, at paras
24-25
;
Canada
Post Corp v Varma
,
2000 CanLII 15754
at para
23
, 192 FTR 278 (FC);
West
Vancouver School District No 45 v Callow
,
2014 ONSC 2547
at para
39
);

c) public records that are a basis for judicial notice (
Wong v
Giannacopoulos
,
2011 ABCA 277
at para
6
, 515 AR 58); and

3.         whether the person has
previously engaged in abusive litigation conduct and/or was declared a
“vexatious litigant” or subject to court access restrictions:
Canada Post
Corp v Varma
, at para
24
;
Canada v Olumide
,
2017 FCA 42
at para
37
,
[2017] GSTC 17

[
108
]

The presence of multiple indicia generally
favours court intervention: e.g.
Chutskoff v Bonora
, at paras
131-132
;
Re
Boisjoli
, at para
104
;
Ewanchuk v Canada (Attorney General)
, at para

158
.

[
109
]

Some forms of litigation misconduct are
particularly serious and merit stringent court responses. For example, abuse of
the
habeas corpus
procedure warrants strict court response due to the
disproportionate negative effect that activity has on court function:
Ewanchuk
v Canada (Attorney General)
, at paras
170-87
;
Re Gauthier
, at para
82.

C.  Positions of the Parties

[
110
]

The Applicants contend that the Plaintiff’s
conduct has been such as to satisfy almost all of the indicia of a vexatious
litigant as described in
Chutskoff v Bonora
, and discussed in 1985
Sawridge
Trust v Alberta (Public Trustee)
,
2017 ABQB 530
.

[
111
]

In argument before me, the Plaintiff did not
directly deny being a vexatious litigant, but placed the blame for her behavior
on the Defendants. She believes that she has been subjected to torment and
humiliation for almost two decades, and is simply doing what she has to do to
secure justice. Ms. Templanza was very clear that this objective remains her
goal.

D.

Assessment

i.

Need for a Vexatious Litigant Declaration

[
112
]

The indicia described in
Chutskoff v Bonora

include:

1.         collateral attacks on adverse
decisions;

2.         bringing hopeless proceedings;

3.         escalating existing procedures
to encompass new litigants and issues;

4.         bringing proceedings for
improper purposes;

5.         failure to abide by Court
imposed obligations;

6.         persistently taking
unsuccessful appeals;

7.         persistently engaging in
inappropriate behavior;

8.         making unsubstantiated
allegations of fraud, conspiracy and misconduct; and

9.         use of scandalous or
inflammatory language in pleading or before the Court.

[
113
]

The presence of many of these indicia of
vexatious litigant is obvious from the recitation of facts and my findings of
fact and law that precede this analysis.

[
114
]

The multiplicity of proceedings brought by the
Plaintiff since becoming self-represented all seek to litigate, in one fashion
or another, Ms. Templanza’s now-dismissed claim against Mr. Wolfman, and her
on-going claim against her son. They are collateral attacks. Ms. Templanza
wants to continue this process. She seeks to add Mr. Wolfman and his firm to
these lawsuits, despite having exhausted her litigation options as against them,
up to the Supreme Court of Canada.

[
115
]

Ms. Templanza’s claims can all be fairly
characterized as hopeless. As I have previously concluded, Ms. Templanza’s
current litigation cannot succeed because her lawsuits are barred by the
Limitations
Act
. Beyond that, her pleadings are often incoherent and incomprehensible.
This can be attributed in part to language barriers. However, the nature of the
claims (e.g. allegations of criminal conspiracy) and the outlandish remedies
sought all point to demands being advanced based on a degree of malice that
cannot be blamed on lack of English language skills.

[
116
]

The Plaintiff has taken many unsuccessful
appeals, and engaged in inappropriate behavior. She has accused opposing
counsel of being “mentally ill”, “thieves” and “extortionists”.

[
117
]

Ms. Templanza has made repeated and unsupported
allegations of fraud and incompetence against the Defendants, opposing counsel,
and members of the judiciary. Her entire case rests on an alleged but
unsubstantiated network of fraud and conspiracy between her son, the Shields,
court actors, and many lawyers.

[
118
]

Among the fraud allegations are disturbing
anti-Semitic comments regarding collusion by current and past Defendants of the
Jewish faith. The excerpts from Ms. Templanza’s documents in this decision also
illustrate her use of scandalous and inflammatory language. I note that in
Ford
v Templanza
,
2015 ABCA 302
, the Court of Appeal concluded that Ms.
Templanza’s documentary materials contained “unfounded, scandalous allegations”,
and granted an order sought by Jason R. Ford to have those parts of the file
sealed from the public because of their inappropriate content.

[
119
]

The Plaintiff has also persisted in attempts to
file pleadings, affidavits and other materials without regard for directions of
this Court. She remains in contempt of this Court in respect of the filing of
the Statements of Claim under consideration here, contrary to a Court order
prohibiting her from doing so while the summary dismissal of her claim against
Mr. Wolfman was being appealed.

[
120
]

In addition to the
Chutskoff v Bonora

criteria, I also note Ms. Templanza has been quite explicit concerning her
intentions. She wants to expand her litigation further, and indicates she is
determined to achieve what she identifies as the just result. That is another
indicium of litigation abuse, where a litigant indicates an intention to engage
in future abuse of court processes:
Lofstrom v Radke
, at para
8
;
Van
Sluytman v Muskoka (District Municipality)
, at paras
23-24
.

[
121
]

Ms. Templanza’s abuse of court processes has not
only occurred in litigation related to the disputed condominium.
Templanza v
Isip
,
2017 ABCA 410
reports Martin JA (as she then was) denying Ms.
Templanza leave to appeal an appeal decision of the Alberta Court of Queen’s
Bench relating to child support arrears. Ms. Templanza was attempting to collect
allegedly unpaid child support due to her daughter: para 3. This was a
‘busybody’ lawsuit (
Chutskoff v Bonora
, para
92
), since Ms. Templanza
had no entitlement to the alleged outstanding child support, which instead was
a claim that belonged to either the grandchildren or their mother: paras 6, 10.

[
122
]

The overall tone and character of the
Templanza
v Isip
litigation appears to parallel that conducted by Ms. Templanza in
relation to the condominium dispute. The courts classified
Templanza v Isip

as “a high conflict situation”: para 4.

[
123
]

It is unfortunate, and in many senses sad, that
the Plaintiff’s behavior in this and other litigation has exhibited many of the
indicia categories that identify litigation abuse. There are many independent
bases on which I could conclude it is time for this Court to intervene.
Collectively, action needs to be taken to address Ms. Templanza’s litigation
activities.

[
124
]

This is ultimately a balancing exercise. Access
to justice is a fundamental value for all Canadians, and is essential to the
operation of a free and democratic society. Such access is threatened by
increased demands on the justice system, limited resources for those
responsible for delivering timely services to the public and increasing cost of
securing legal counsel.

[
125
]

Access to the courts is also threatened when
individual Canadians abuse the legal system by improperly advancing claims, triggering
a disproportionate demand on the time of the judiciary, Court staff, and
opposing litigants. As Stratas JA recently observed in
Canada v Olumide
,
at paras
17-21
, courts are a limited community property that exist to serve
everyone.

[
126
]

There is no question in this case that the
Plaintiff believes that she was treated unfairly by everyone involved in her
unsuccessful attempt to purchase a condominium, including friends, family and
her lawyer. She may or may not be right about that, and she may still have an available
remedy under her action against Mr. Gabriel.

[
127
]

However, that does not entitle or justify the
initiation of an ever-widening web of lawsuits that would seek to litigate the unfairness
of that conduct, but within a framework of imagined conspiracies among people
who had a little or nothing to do with the unsuccessful condominium purchase,
so many years ago.

ii.

Scope of Vexatious Litigant Declaration

[
128
]

Following the
Hok v Alberta
approach, my
first question is to ask is whether Ms. Templanza can be anticipated to engage
in future litigation abuse. Her history establishes that, and she is direct
about what she intends to do.

[
129
]

The next question is whether Ms. Templanza’s
problematic litigation activities will plausibly remain sequestered within a
certain dispute or with a set of parties, or may be confined to a particular
court. That obviously is not the case. Ms. Templanza is engaged in problematic
activity in all Alberta courts, and in multiple disputes. Further, her
litigation pattern is one of ‘escalation’, where she adds additional parties.

[
130
]

On that basis I have no difficulty in concluding
that a broad-based court access restriction regime is appropriate for Ms.
Templanza, where her activities are regulated globally and in all three Alberta
Courts. I will therefore require that Ms. Templanza obtain leave from the
appropriate administrative judge or justice prior to initiating or continuing
any action, application, appeal, or proceeding in the Alberta Court of Appeal,
Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench, and Provincial Court of Alberta.

[
131
]

This is a comparatively minor limitation to a
litigant’s access to court processes (
Hok v Alberta
, at paras 32-33;
Wong
v Giannacopoulos
, at para
8
), proportional given that “[t]here is no
constitutional right to bring frivolous or vexatious cases” (
Trial Lawyers
Association of British Columbia
, at para
47
), and does not cause “undue
hardship” that effectively blocks access to court relief (
Trial Lawyers
Association of British Columbia
, at paras
45-48
).

[
132
]

That said, I believe it is also necessary to
consider a more stringent and unusual step to address Ms. Templanza’s court
activities. This Court in certain instances has also required that any leave
application to initiate or continue litigation must be filed by a lawyer:
Re
Boisjoli
, at paras
108-109
;
Ewanchuk v Canada (Attorney General)
, at
paras
185-197
;
Re Gauthier
, at para 83;
Onischuk v Edmonton (City)
,
at paras
15-16
;
Onischuk (Re)
,
at para
66
. Wakeling JA recently in
Re
Gauthier
,
2018 ABCA 14
at paras
11-18
confirmed this step is a valid tool
when this Court under its inherent jurisdiction responds to anticipated abuse
of court processes.

[
133
]

I conclude that this step is also appropriate
for Ms. Templanza, despite the fact that it will plausibly impose an additional
financial burden on her. First, lawyer representation during filing a leave
application is necessary as an additional screen to help control Ms.
Templanza’s plausible response to being forced to seek leave to initiate or
continue her civil proceedings.

[
134
]

As the case management justice in these matters
I have become familiar with Ms. Templanza’s problematic approach to court
proceedings. Ms. Templanza has proven to be a very active litigant. She has an
established pattern of ignoring court instructions and orders. This combination
warrants the Court ordering her file any leave application via a lawyer.

[
135
]

Second, this requirement will assist Ms.
Templanza to frame her new or continuing actions in their best possible light.
I have previously observed that she may have valid bases to seek remedies in
this and other Alberta Courts. One of the ongoing problems with Ms. Templanza’s
actions is that they lack focus and revolve around unsubstantiated
results-based allegations, rather than the necessary information to establish a
potentially valid cause of action.

[
136
]

In
Re Thompson
,
2018 ABQB 87
, Justice
Nielsen explained that once a person is subject to a court access restrictions
then that person is
presumed
to engage in illegitimate litigation,
unless the court is satisfied otherwise: para 19. An abusive litigant subject
to that presumption has the obligation to establish a foundation for their
application, and put their “best foot forward” to displace that presumption:
para 27.

[
137
]

I believe Ms. Templanza would greatly benefit
from legal assistance in putting her “best foot forward”. If she has legitimate
causes of action, the requirement that a lawyer is involved in filing her leave
applications will assist. That way the issues and relevant facts are more
likely to be identified and presented in a useful manner. In the long run that
will benefit both the Courts and Ms. Templanza by establishing a more
productive litigation pattern. Given Ms. Templanza’s history of bringing action
against legal counsel, court access restrictions may also make it easier for
Ms. Templanza to find counsel in the future as they too would be protected
against subsequent actions by her.

[
138
]

In light of
Templanza v Isip
I will also
prohibit Ms. Templanza from acting as litigation representative in any form.

[
139
]

The Court is responsible to ensure persons who
appear before it are properly represented, and, more generally, to maintain the
integrity of the court process:
R v Dick
,
2002 BCCA 27
at paras
6-7
, 163
BCAC 62;
Peddle v Alberta Treasury Branches
,
2004 ABQB 608
, 133 ACWS
(3d) 253;
Gauthier v Starr
,
2016 ABQB 213
at paras
54-56
, 86 CPC (7th)
348. Ms. Templanza’s troubling and ongoing abuse of court processes means she
is not an appropriate in-court representative.

[
140
]

I therefore order:

1.         Ms. Templanza is prohibited
from acting as an agent, next friend, McKenzie Friend (from
McKenzie v
McKenzie
,
[1970] 3 All ER 1034 (UK CA)
and
Alberta Rules of Court
, ss
2.22-2.23), or any other form of representative in court proceedings before the
Alberta Provincial Court, Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench, and Alberta Court of
Appeal.

2.         The Clerks of the Alberta
Provincial Court, Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench, and Alberta Court of Appeal
shall refuse to accept or file any documents or other materials from Ms. Templanza,
in a representative capacity.

[
141
]

Since there is no constitutional right to act as
a court representative, a restriction of this kind is always appropriate where
a person exhibits bad litigation practices as a litigation representative:
Gauthier
v Starr
, at paras
55-56
.

E.   Court Restriction Order

[
142
]

It is both necessary and timely to issue an
order that restricts Ms. Templanza’s access to the Alberta Court of Appeal,
Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench, and Provincial Court.

[
143
]

The Court therefore responds to the Application
by exercising its inherent jurisdiction, and, on its own motion under that
authority, declares that Rosalina Templanza is a vexatious litigant and orders:

1.         Rosaline Templanza is
prohibited, under the inherent jurisdiction of the Court of Queen’s Bench of
Alberta, from commencing, or attempting to commence, or continuing any appeal, action,
application, or proceeding in the Alberta Court of Appeal, Court of Queen’s Bench
of Alberta, or the Provincial Court of Alberta, on her own behalf or on behalf of
any other person or estate, without an order of the Chief Justice or Associate
Chief Justice, or Chief Judge, of the Court in which the proceeding is conducted,
or his or her designate.

2.         The Chief Justice or Associate
Chief Justice, or Chief Judge, or his or her designate, may, at any time,
direct that notice of an application to commence or continue an appeal, action,
application, or proceeding be given to any other person.

3.         Rosalina Templanza must
describe herself, in the application or document to which this Order applies,
as “Rosalina Templanza”, and not by using initials, an alternative name
structure, or a pseudonym.

4.         Any application for leave by Rosalina
Templanza will only be accepted if Rosalina Templanza is represented by a member
in good standing of the Law Society of Alberta.

5.         This Order does not apply to
any appeal of this decision to the Alberta Court of Appeal.

6.         Any application to commence or
continue any appeal, action, application, or proceeding must be accompanied by
an affidavit:

(i) attaching a copy of the Order arising from this Decision,
restricting Rosalina Templanza’s access to the Alberta Court of Appeal, Court of
Queen’s Bench of Alberta, and Provincial Court of Alberta;

(ii) attaching a copy of the appeal, pleading, application, or
process that Rosalina Templanza proposes to issue or file or continue;

(iii) deposing fully and completely to the facts and circumstances surrounding
the proposed claim or proceeding, so as to demonstrate that the proceeding is not
an abuse of process, and that there are reasonable grounds for it;

(iv) indicating whether Rosalina Templanza has ever sued some or all
of the defendants or respondents previously in any jurisdiction or Court, and if
so providing full particulars;

(v) undertaking that, if leave is granted, the authorized appeal,
pleading, application or process, the Order granting leave to proceed, and the affidavit
in support of the Order will promptly be served on the defendants or
respondents; and

(vi) undertaking to diligently prosecute the proceeding.

7.         Any application referenced
herein shall be made in writing.

8.         The Chief Justice or Associate
Chief Justice, or Chief Judge, or his or her designate, may:

(i) give notice of the proposed claim or proceeding and the
opportunity to make submissions on the proposed claim or proceeding, if they so
choose, to:

a) the involved or potentially involved parties;

b) other relevant persons identified by the Court; and

c) the Attorney Generals of Alberta and Canada;

(ii) respond to and or dispose of the leave application in writing;
and

(iii) hold the application in open Court where it shall be recorded.

9.         Leave to commence or continue
proceedings may be given on conditions, including the posting of security for costs,
and proof of payment of all prior cost awards.

10.       An application that is dismissed
may not be made again, directly or indirectly.

11.       Any application to vary this Order
shall be made on notice to the Attorney General and any other person as directed
by the Court hearing that application.

12.       This Order does not apply to
Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench Action No. 0701-06304 (
Templanza v Gabriel
),
unless Ms. Templanza seeks to amend such claim to add additional defendant(s).

13.       The Court shall prepare the Order
arising from this decision.

14.       Pursuant to
Rule
9.2(4) the
approval of Rosalina Templanza as to the form and content of the Order is not
required.

[
144
]

This Order takes effect immediately, and is
being issued in a stand-alone form in conjunction with this Judgment.

[
145
]

In argument, I was advised by counsel for the
Applicant that the Attorney General of Alberta has not yet been provided a copy
of the proposed vexatious litigant declaration, per
Judicature Act
, s
23.1(1). As I have previously indicated, I have proceeded to limit Ms.
Templanza’s court access under this Court’s inherent jurisdiction, rather than
the
Judicature Act
provisions.

[
146
]

Nevertheless, and in an excess of caution, I am
suspending
permanent
operation of the court access restriction order
against Ms. Templanza for a period of thirty days. The Applicant shall within
five days serve the Attorney General copies of:

1.         Mr. Todd Lee’s application that
Ms. Templanza be declared a vexatious litigant and subject to court access
restrictions per
Judicature Act
, ss 23-23.1;

2          this decision; and

3.         the Order prepared by the Court
that restricts Ms. Templanza’s access to Alberta courts.

[
147
]

The Attorney General may provide written
comments on the final form of Order within 21 days of service. In fairness to
Ms. Templanza and the Applicants, I will also permit them to provide written
comments to the Court on the final form of Order within 21 days of service. Written
comments shall not exceed five pages.

[
148
]

Should written comments be received a follow-up
case management meeting may be scheduled to hear submissions from the parties,
and permanent operation of the Order will be further suspended to allow that
process to be completed.

[
149
]

If no submissions are received then the
vexatious litigant, and court access restriction order will become permanent,
in accordance with its terms.

IX.

Security for Costs Application

[
150
]

As the actions against the Defendants are
summarily dismissed, there is no need to decide the applications for
alternative relief in the form of Security for Costs.

X.

Conclusion

[
151
]

The claims by Ms. Templanza against each of the
Defendant lawyers (and their respective law firms) are summarily dismissed. The
application of Mr. Todd Lee to have Ms. Templanza declared a vexatious litigant
is granted. Ms. Templanza is therefore prohibited from initiating or continuing
actions in the Alberta Court of Appeal, Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench, and the
Provincial Court of Alberta, except with leave of the appropriate Chief
Justice, Associate Chief Justice, Chief Judge, or his or her designate. This
prohibition does not include an appeal of this decision nor does it apply to
Action No. 0701-06304 (
Templanza v Gabriel
), unless Ms. Templanza seeks
to amend that application to include new respondent(s).

[
152
]

The Applicants are entitled to costs on Column 2
in respect of the Summary Dismissal applications and in respect of the
Vexatious Litigant application. If the parties cannot agree on costs within
sixty days, the matter may be directed to me for determination by way of
written submissions, not to exceed five pages in length.
